text:
Recent work supports perturbation probes but cautions against equating order sensitivity with intent understanding. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compares original and shuffled histories across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) contrasts random shuffling with shuffling constrained by item availability: apparent sequential signal can reflect catalog evolution rather than user behavior. [Spotify’s 2026 study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) investigates whether contextual sequence encoders improve over simpler transition models, including recency-weighted aggregation. Together, these motivate controls for item popularity, availability, and last-item effects before attributing ranking changes to higher-order intent modeling.

Intent-focused methods offer complementary hypotheses. [Temporal-Aware and Intent Contrastive Learning (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/17/10/1634) warns that random augmentation can disrupt sequential semantics; [MIMAR-SRec (2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) models intent across temporal windows and trains against interaction, temporal, and preference noise. Suggested diagnostic synthesis: use training-only next-item pseudo-holdouts with fixed candidate sets; compare recent-item deletion against equal-count older/random deletion, full shuffling against last-item-preserving shuffling, and repeated-theme removal against frequency-matched controls. Derive themes only from available titles/descriptions. Report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, and top-10 overlap by category and history length, with user-level uncertainty estimates. These measure reliance and robustness—not observed intent or causal correctness. Weak recent-deletion effects suggest limited recency use; strong shuffle effects without predictive gains suggest brittle positional dependence. Compare recency weighting, sequence encoding, and training objectives through controlled ablations.
